title: Aristotle

cards.b:
Aristotle (384–322 BCE) studied in Plato's Academy for about twenty years and later tutored Alexander the Great. He founded his own school, the Lyceum.

Where Plato looked up at ideal Forms, Aristotle looked around at real states. His students are said to have gathered the constitutions of 158 Greek cities. Only The Constitution of the Athenians survives.

That is why he is called the father of political science. He is one of the most-asked thinkers in Paper I.

In the Politics, Aristotle says man is by nature a political animal (zoon politikon). We can only become fully human inside a polis.

He who lives without a state, he says, is "either a beast or a god".

The state grows naturally: first the household, then the village, then the polis. The polis comes into being for the sake of life, but it continues for the sake of the good life.

So the state is not an artificial contract. It is natural, and it is prior to the individual, as the whole is prior to its parts.

Aristotle explains things by their telos, or end. An acorn's telos is the oak. A human being's telos is eudaimonia: flourishing, a life of virtue and reason.

The state's job is to make that flourishing possible. It is a moral community, not just a security pact or a trade deal.

This is the key contrast with liberals like Locke, for whom the state only protects rights. For Aristotle, the state must make citizens good.

Aristotle uses two tests: how many rule, and in whose interest. Note that for him "democracy" is the bad form: rule by the poor for themselves.

He adds that oligarchy and democracy really differ by wealth, not numbers: rule of the rich versus rule of the poor.

Aristotle's best practical state is polity, a mix of oligarchy and democracy.

It works best when there is a large middle class. The very rich grow arrogant and the very poor grow resentful. The middle class is moderate, and it can hold the balance.

This follows his ethics of the golden mean: virtue lies between extremes, as courage lies between cowardice and rashness.

Revolutions happen, he says in Book V, mainly because people feel unequally treated. A strong middle keeps a state stable.

Who is a citizen?

A citizen is one who shares in ruling and being ruled in turn: who takes part in judging and holding office. Women, slaves, foreigners and manual workers were excluded.

Distributive justice

Treat equals equally and unequals unequally, in proportion to merit. Offices should go to those who add most to the good life of the state.

Corrective justice

Restores balance when one person wrongs another, as in a court case.

Aristotle defends natural slavery: some people, he claims, lack full reasoning and are best ruled by a master. He admits that some slaves are enslaved only by war and law, which he finds harder to defend.

He defends private property against Plato. People care more for what is their own, and owning things lets us practise generosity. But use should be shared, and wealth-making for its own sake (chrematistics) is unnatural.

He also defends the family as natural, and rejects Plato's communism of wives.

cards.h: Aristotle against Plato, and his critics
cards.b:
• Against Plato: the ideal state seeks too much unity. A state is a plurality; make it too much one and it becomes a household.
  • His defence of slavery and the exclusion of women are now rejected. Feminists like Susan Moller Okin show how his idea of "nature" was used to justify hierarchy.
  • His citizenship suits a small city, not a mass modern state.
  • Yet thinkers like Alasdair MacIntyre and Martha Nussbaum revived his ideas of virtue and flourishing.

His middle-class thesis is used to explain democratic stability: a growing Indian middle class is often linked to demands for better governance.

His proportional idea of justice helps explain Article 14. The Supreme Court allows reasonable classification: treating unequals differently is not discrimination, if the basis is fair.

Amartya Sen's capability approach, which Nussbaum ties to Aristotle's idea of flourishing, shaped the UNDP's Human Development Index (1990).

"Aristotle is the father of political science." Comment.
"Discuss Aristotle's classification of governments and his idea of polity."
"Compare Plato's and Aristotle's views on property."

Structure: show his empirical method (158 constitutions), the natural state and the good life, draw the six-fold table, then make polity and the middle class your highlight. End with his modern revival in virtue ethics.

quiz.q: For Aristotle, the polis continues to exist for the sake of…
quiz.w: The state arises for life but continues for the good life.

quiz.q: In Aristotle's scheme, the perverted form of rule by the many is…
quiz.w: Polity is the true form; democracy is rule by the poor in their own interest.

quiz.q: Aristotle's best practical state relies on…
quiz.w: Polity is stable when a large middle class holds the balance.

quiz.q: A citizen for Aristotle is one who…
o: Shares in ruling and being ruled in turn
quiz.w: Citizenship means taking part in judging and holding office.

quiz.q: Aristotle's main objection to Plato's ideal state was that it…
o: Gave too much power to the poor
quiz.w: He argued a state is a plurality, and too much unity destroys it.
